Hair Growth. The natural hair is considered as an extension of the skin and is a body part where hair can grow. Hair growth can be defined as the process of new hairs growing from the dermal papilla or hair follicle into the skin. Hair growth consists of three phases: the anagen (growth), catagen (transitional phase), and telogen (decretion). The catagen and telogen phases are not considered as phases of hair growth, rather as resting phases. The active phase of the hair cycle is called anagen.[1] The anagen phase is followed by the catagen phase with a duration of 2 weeks. The catagen phase, in turn, is followed by a resting phase called the telogen (or telogen phase or resting phase). The anagen and catagen phases are active (hair growth) while the telogen phase is dormant and hair loss does not occur. During the telogen phase of the cycle, the hair follicle regenerates and becomes active again in the next anagen phase. The average duration of the telogen phase and the duration of the anagen phase differs among regions and among ethnicities. Hair grows about 1 centimeter per month
